abstracts.abstract: Classical numerical analysis has traditionally relied on worst-case backward error analysis to characterize algorithm behavior. This paper introduces a novel probabilistic framework for theoretical analysis of numerical algorithms that fundamentally reconceptualizes how we understand rounding error propagation. Rather than treating floating-point roundoff as deterministic bounded quantities, we model individual rounding errors as independent random variables with known statistical distributions, enabling the derivation of probabilistic tail bounds on forward error. This paradigm shift from deterministic to probabilistic error analysis reveals that many established numerical algorithms exhibit inherent statistical error cancellation properties that classical theory fails to capture. We develop comprehensive probabilistic perturbation theory for fundamental linear algebra operations including matrix multiplication, LU factorization, and QR decomposition. The derived error bounds demonstrate remarkable accuracy compared to traditional worst-case estimates while providing richer information about error distribution. This framework establishes a new paradigm for numerical algorithm analysis that enables more accurate error prediction, adaptive algorithm selection based on actual rather than theoretical error behavior, and theoretically grounded probabilistic stopping criteria for iterative methods. The approach bridges numerical analysis with statistical learning theory, opening new research directions in uncertainty quantification for scientific computing.

Perturbation analysis for eigenvalue problems has traditionally relied on classical Bauer-Fike theory, which provides general but often overly pessimistic bounds for structured matrices. This paper presents refined perturbation bounds for eigenvalue solvers operating on structured matrices arising frequently in scientific computing applications. By exploiting spectral properties including normality, definiteness, and low-rank structure, we derive theoretical bounds that are significantly tighter than existing results. Our analysis introduces a new condition number formulation that captures the interaction between matrix structure and eigenvalue sensitivity, revealing that classical condition numbers overestimate sensitivity by factors ranging from O(1) to O(n) depending on matrix structure. For Hermitian matrices, we prove that standard Rayleigh quotient iteration exhibits second-order convergence with an improved asymptotic constant. For normal matrices, we establish enhanced backward stability results demonstrating that most algorithms achieve full backward stability in practice despite theoretical limitations. The theoretical improvements are validated through extensive numerical experiments on test matrices from practical applications including structural dynamics, quantum chemistry, and machine learning. These refined bounds provide more reliable stopping criteria for iterative eigenvalue solvers and enable more accurate a priori error estimation in computational workflows requiring eigenvalue computations.

The design of software for numerical solution of differential equations has historically followed either equation-specific monolithic architectures or ad-hoc reuse strategies with limited flexibility. This paper presents a novel software architecture for differential equation solvers based on the principle of structural composition, fundamentally reconceptualizing mathematical software design for initial value problems and boundary value problems. The architecture separates mathematical abstraction layers from computational implementation through a carefully designed interface hierarchy that enables arbitrary composition of numerical methods, time integrators, and linear solvers. We introduce the concept of method descriptors that declaratively specify numerical algorithms in terms of composable mathematical properties, enabling automatic code generation and optimization for diverse problem classes. The software system implements a comprehensive library of explicit and implicit Runge-Kutta methods, linear multistep methods, and hybrid solvers with adaptive step size control. Novel contributions include automatic differentiation of composed methods for Jacobian computation, sophisticated error estimation for method selection, and parallel-in-time integration capabilities. Implementation demonstrates that the compositional approach achieves performance competitive with specialized hand-optimized solvers while providing unprecedented flexibility for algorithm exploration and domain-specific customization in scientific computing applications.

Sparse matrix operations constitute critical computational kernels in large-scale scientific computing, yet existing libraries often sacrifice performance for generality or vice versa. This paper presents a comprehensive software framework for high-performance sparse matrix computations that significantly advances the state of the art in both performance and functionality. The framework introduces novel data structures optimized for modern hierarchical memory architectures combined with cache-oblivious algorithms for sparse matrix-vector multiplication, triangular solve, and factorization operations. Key algorithmic innovations include automatic format selection based on matrix structure analysis, runtime optimization of computational kernels for specific sparsity patterns, and intelligent prefetching strategies that exploit data reuse patterns. We describe a complete implementation supporting multiple sparse matrix formats including CSR, CSC, COO, ELL, and hybrid formats with automatic format conversion. Performance evaluation on representative benchmark matrices demonstrates speedups of 1.8-4.2x over Intel MKL and SuiteSparse libraries for key operations. The software framework includes sophisticated numerical stability monitoring, memory usage optimization, and profiling tools that enable practitioners to understand and optimize sparse matrix computation performance. Extensive testing infrastructure ensures correctness verification across diverse matrix collections, establishing new standards for reliability in mathematical software.
